title: UNCERTAINTY-AWARE LIQUID STATE MODELING FROM EXPERIMENTAL SCATTERING MEASUREMENTS

Instead, the provided text is a 2025 chemistry/physics dissertation-preprint by Brennon L. Shanks on liquid-state modeling from neutron and X-ray scattering data. The dissertation addresses a scientific inverse problem: how to infer interatomic forces and thermodynamic properties of dense fluids from experimental scattering measurements while rigorously accounting for uncertainty. The core question is whether Bayesian uncertainty quantification and probabilistic machine learning can improve structure-potential modeling for liquids beyond prior methods such as empirical potential structure refinement (EPSR) and related statistical-mechanics approaches.

The approach is methodological and theoretical rather than educational or intervention-based. Across the dissertation, the author proposes uncertainty-aware techniques including probabilistic iterative potential refinement using Gaussian process regression, accelerated Bayesian uncertainty quantification for reconstructed pair potentials, and Bayesian analysis of how experimental neutron-scattering error propagates into force-field estimation. The text also reproduces prior published chemistry papers as dissertation chapters, including work on machine-learning-assisted structure refinement and local Gaussian process surrogate models. Its context is graduate research in chemical engineering and statistical mechanics, not a school-based AI writing-feedback implementation.

The dissertation discusses simulations, noble-liquid systems, neutron-scattering measurements, and theoretical developments in liquid-state physics. No secondary students, teachers, classrooms, or educational institutions as study sites are reported. Because the user's retrieval target was a 2025 study on AI-assisted writing feedback for secondary students, the strongest evidence-based resolution from the provided text is that this is a false retrieval or metadata mismatch: the title, author, domain, and content do not correspond to the target education study.

The main conclusions of the actual document are that rigorous Bayesian uncertainty quantification can improve interpretation of scattering data, help reconstruct interaction potentials while maintaining thermodynamic consistency, and clarify when experimental noise limits recovery of interatomic forces. The author argues that liquid-state structural analysis is more useful and nuanced than previously believed. However, none of these conclusions bear on AI-assisted writing feedback or secondary students' writing skills.
